problem: Which of the following shows some of the solution curves of the differential equation ${x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+1=0$ for $x>0?$

examples.knowledge_point: Sketching the Solution Curves of a Differential Equation
examples.problem: Solve the differential equation $y'  = 2x,$ and sketch the solution curves of this equation.
examples.worked_solution:
Integrating the equation, we get

$$
y = x^2+C.
$$

We can now plot the solution curves by selecting different values for $C.$ The sketch below shows the solution curves for $C=-2,0,1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14011667/assets/e37771799ef5fadc259e6ea0073042a83e0974b5a2619d1af3e87a7467e6d780.png)

feedback.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=6{x}^{2}-4x.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (6{x}^{2}-4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-4\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-4(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+C \\  & =2{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+C)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =2\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x-2\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =2(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})-2(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$
